label: explain2-track-4
one_line: We will print 21 spinning seed models, drop them in water, and test whether a published computer model or a simple rule better predicts how fast they sink.
what: Some trees make fruit with two curved wings. When it falls, the fruit spins like a helicopter blade. Scientists call this spinning fall "autorotation". It just means the fruit turns by itself as it drops. Researchers 3D-printed copies of such fruit. They dropped the copies in a tall tank of water. We want to write down our guesses first. Then we will print 21 new shapes and drop them. We have two guesses to compare. The first is a published computer model. It cuts each wing into thin strips and adds up the push of the water on every strip. The second is a much simpler rule, built by the earlier designer. It is a short formula with one number you can adjust. The test measures how fast each model sinks at a steady speed. It does not measure sideways gliding. So far this is only a plan. We have no new results.
why: Spinning fruit fall slowly. So wind can carry the seeds away from the parent tree. If we can predict the best wing curve, we learn how a simple shape gets good flight. This test also checks a published model. We write our guess before we look, so nobody can say we tuned it afterwards. A miss would be useful too. We do not claim this will help medicine or machines yet.

steps.text: Download the public data and the model code from the research group. Both are free to reuse under the MIT licence.
steps.picture: Borrowing a recipe book that the cook says anyone may copy.

steps.text: Redo the earlier arithmetic from scratch. Every number we checked came out the same, apart from tiny rounding.
steps.picture: Adding up a restaurant bill a second time and getting the same total.

steps.text: Write down what the computer model predicts for each of 21 new wing shapes. Then seal the file. Sealing means saving it so it cannot be changed. We do this before any drop happens. For example, an invented prediction might read: 'this shape sinks at 8 centimetres per second'.
steps.picture: Calling the score before the match starts.

steps.text: Write down what the simple rival rule predicts for the same shapes. It is the earlier designer's own rule. It is not a proven law.
steps.picture: Asking a second friend to guess the score too.

steps.text: Print the 21 shapes. Each differs in how curved the wings are. Each also differs in the tilt of the wing root. The root is the spot where the wing joins the seed. Tilt is the angle of that join.
steps.picture: Baking 21 loaves, each with a slightly different shape.

steps.text: Drop each shape in a tall water tank and time its steady sinking speed. That is the constant speed it reaches once it stops speeding up. Repeat the drops, because copies of the same shape differ by a few percent. We do not yet know how many repeats we will do.
steps.picture: Dropping the same stone many times to see how much the timing wobbles.

steps.text: Compare the sealed guesses with the measured speeds. Say the invented guess was 8 centimetres per second and the tank gave 7. We then ask whether that 1 centimetre gap is bigger than the usual scatter between copies. Count a win only if it is.
steps.picture: Two runners are only separate if they finish further apart than the stopwatch error.

steps.text: Publish the result, including a miss. We also plan a second test with a flat plate that really glides sideways.
steps.picture: Telling the team both the wins and the flops.

wrong_if: Here is our bet, written before we look. The model should pick the right wing curve. It should also put the shapes with a tilted root in the right order of speed. We call the model wrong if it misses by more than the usual scatter between copies of one shape. If the simple rule does as well, the strip model adds nothing. Old public data already hint at this. We fitted the simple rule to ten sets of old data. That means we adjusted it afterwards to match them. Its average miss was 0.055. The model's was 0.088. The miss is measured as a ratio, so smaller is better. Think of about 5.5 percent against 8.8 percent. These were fits to old data. They were not guesses made in advance.
could_go_wrong: The test measures sinking speed, not sideways gliding. So our glide-distance rule does not apply to it.
The published model is partly tuned. Its drag was reduced and its weight set to 1.2 grams. So it was not a pure prediction.
Copies of one shape differ by a few percent. That can make a close contest end in a tie.
The simple rival rule is the earlier designer's own construction. It may be a weak or unfair opponent.

At a root tilt of 15 degrees, the model and the rival differ by only about 6.5 percent. Two repeat rounds of the same shape at zero tilt already differ by about 7 percent. So the gap we want to see is no bigger than the noise.
The published experiments used only two tilts, 0 and 35 degrees. So there is no data at all for 15 degrees.
One of our planned checks may be too easy. It might pass whatever happens, so it would prove nothing. We could not find the file that sets it, so we cannot say for sure.
The public data could change if the repository owner updates it.

questions.q: How do you know the earlier numbers are right?
questions.a: We downloaded the files again. We checked their fingerprints, which are short codes that change if the file changes. Then we re-ran the sums. The results matched, apart from tiny rounding. That shows the numbers were read correctly. It does not show the physics idea is right.

We have not printed or dropped a single new fruit. We have not tested a tilt of 15 degrees in water. We did not re-run every computer simulation the reviewers used. Some of the test design files we could not find.

questions.q: Why drop things in water instead of air?
questions.a: The researchers used a tall tank of water. The flow in water behaves like fast air around a larger seed. Water also makes the fall slow enough to time.

questions.q: How many times is each shape dropped?
questions.a: We do not know yet. The plan only says the drops are repeated. The number is not fixed in the facts we have.

questions.q: What does the wing fold number mean, and what does tilt do?
questions.a: The fold value is a number for how curved the wing is. The tilt is the angle where the wing joins the seed. In the public data, the same fruit shape sank at 0.1011 metres per second with no tilt. At a 35 degree tilt it sank at 0.0676 metres per second. That is about 10 centimetres per second against 7. The first is a slow walk across a kitchen. So tilting the root made the fruit sink about 1.5 times slower.

No. A spinning fruit sinks nearly straight down. We read our glide-distance rule as giving zero for it, so it says nothing here. That is why we also plan a flat-plate glider test. A flat plate is a thin sheet that can drift sideways as it falls.

questions.q: Do real fruits match the best curve?
questions.a: Partly. We have data on 27 wild fruits, meaning fruits gathered from trees outside the lab. Their average fold value was 1.8, with about 10 percent measurement error. That sits near the model's best value for one tilt. The tilt of each real fruit was not reported, so we do not know more.

questions.q: Does wind carry real fruit as far as a simple sum says?
questions.a: No. A simple wind-drift sum came out about 4 to 8 times too far for twelve tropical fruit species. The middle value was about 7 times. Real fruits land much closer to the tree. We do not use this sum in the test.

questions.q: Why does the glide rule matter at all?
questions.a: It is a side thread and does not change the test. Our project keeps a list of rules, and each rule has a maths proof checked by a computer. One rule links wing shape to gliding. Long, thin wings glide further, but only up to a limit. It assumes a standard simple drag model. So it is a limit, not a measurement.

questions.q: Who disagrees on why spinning seeds fall slowly?
questions.a: One account says a small whirl of air sticks to the front edge of the wing and adds lift. The other fits a simple curve to measurements. The model we chose uses the curve, not the whirl.

glossary.plain: Spinning by itself while falling, like a helicopter blade that is not powered.
Made by a machine that builds a shape from plastic, layer by layer.
A set of sums on a computer that guesses what will happen.
A method that adds up the push of air or water on many thin slices of a wing.
A short formula with one adjustable number that guesses the sinking speed.
The simple rule we compare against the strip model.
The angle at which the wing joins the body of the fruit.
A number for how curved the wing is.
The small differences between copies of the same shape.
A second round of drops with the same shape.
The constant speed a fruit reaches once it stops speeding up.
The tall water container the drops happen in.
A number that tells how smooth or swirly a flow is. Bigger means more swirl. It appears only in a check command below.
How far a glider travels forward for each unit of height it drops.
The push of air or water that slows a moving thing.
The push that holds a wing up or sideways against its fall.
A small tornado of air that clings to the front edge of a wing.

glossary.term: log error (miss on a ratio scale)
glossary.plain: A way to measure how far off a guess is, by ratio rather than by plain difference. Smaller is better.
Adjusted after the fact so the numbers match old data.
A permission that lets anyone reuse the files for free.
Guesses saved before the test so they cannot be changed afterwards.
A short code that changes if even one byte of a file changes.
A program that checks a maths proof line by line.
Our list of rules a design must obey. Each rule has a maths proof checked by a computer.
A flat sheet with a weight at the front that flutters, glides or dives.
Fruit gathered from trees outside the lab.

check_yourself.what: Re-run the analysis on the downloaded public data.
check_yourself.expect: Output equal to the file expected_output.txt. For example: sinking speed 0.0676, tilt ratio 1.495, and the lowest Reynolds number (swirl measure) 4352 at fold value 1.805.

check_yourself.what: Print the measured speeds and compute the ratio between the 0 and 35 degree tilts.
check_yourself.expect: Rows with speeds 0.1011 and 0.0676 metres per second, and a ratio of about 1.496.

check_yourself.what: Check the new maths proof about wing shape and glide ratio.
check_yourself.expect: errors=0 sorryAx=0 and the line ALL CHECKED: no errors, no sorryAx.
A glide ratio of 3.77 at 0.220 chord and 14.9 degrees, and no balance point at 0.30.

check_yourself.what: Download the public repository and compare its fingerprint.
check_yourself.expect: 3065098 bytes, sha256 starting c9c2d661, unless the repository has changed.

left_out: Claim that the test is inconclusive about 84 percent of the time if the strip model is true: it comes from the agent's own simulation with assumed scatter, which the checker could not re-run.
Claim that one comparison cannot fail as written: the rule text lives in a design file the checker could not find, so it is left out as fact.
Claim that the model's tilt ratio is 1.22 against 1.50 measured: the 1.22 is only an earlier agent's own number that the checker did not recompute.
Claim that 1.2 grams versus 2.16 grams and a halved drag are exact: the paper only says drag was reduced, so no exact factor is stated.
Claim that the zero glide range for a vertical sinker is a fact of the rule: the zero is the agent's own assumption, so it is stated only as our reading.
The 0.33 to 0.57 expected band for the strip model: it rests on the agent's own assumptions about the density of the lead weights and the mass of the key, so it is left out.
